raw_response.printed_headline_estimate: N = 129 Grade 7 learners (76 female, 53 male) across 5 primary schools. Demographic-only inferential comparisons (Table 4 & Section 3.2, PDF pp. 6-7): Hygiene Access Index male mean 46.75% (median 45.45, IQR 36.36-54.55) vs female mean 39.10% (median 36.36, IQR 27.27-54.55), p = 0.008; Hygiene Access Index younger learners (44.07%) vs older learners (38.27%), p = 0.010; Water Access Index overall mean 53.75% (95% CI: 51.33-56.17; gender contrast p = 0.433); Sanitation Access Index overall mean 56.50% (95% CI: 52.74-60.26; gender contrast p = 0.341); Sanitation Privacy Index overall mean 53.34% (95% CI: 50.43-56.24; gender contrast p = 0.683).
raw_response.publication_year_note: Published 26 May 2026 in Sustainability 2026, Volume 18, Issue 11, Article 5333 (Received: 6 April 2026; Revised: 22 May 2026; Accepted: 22 May 2026).
raw_response.rationale: The study conducts a cross-sectional survey of 129 Grade 7 learners (all of whom had prior WASH training per inclusion criteria) across five purposively selected primary schools in eThekwini District, South Africa, using Chi-square, Fisher's exact, and Kruskal-Wallis tests alongside 95% confidence intervals for composite WASH index means. However, all inferential hypothesis tests compare WASH index scores exclusively across learner demographic characteristics (gender and age: e.g., Hygiene Access Index female vs male p = 0.008; younger vs older learners p = 0.010; Water/Sanitation Access gender p = 0.433 and p = 0.341). No legal, regulatory, tenure, tariff, ownership, governance, or institutional/external-assistance exposure is quantitatively contrasted (failing Criterion 2), and school-level maintenance and supply-chain observations across the five schools are reported only descriptively. Thus, the inferential estimates are out of scope for SWiM synthesis.
